# Diagnosing RPM Loss on a Briggs & Stratton Push Mower

When a 21-inch Craftsman push mower equipped with a 7 hp Briggs & Stratton engine struggles to maintain RPMs in thick grass, it is rarely because the engine has lost its horsepower rating. Instead, you are likely dealing with a mismatch between the available torque and the load imposed by the cutting deck. Since your recent blade sharpening provided immediate relief, you have already addressed one of the most critical friction points; however, the persistence of power loss suggests deeper issues within the air-fuel mixture or mechanical resistance.

The first area to investigate is the carburetor, specifically the idle and high-speed jets. Over six years of operation, even with regular oil changes, fuel varnish and carbon deposits can clog these tiny passages. When the engine encounters resistance from thick grass, it drops below its normal operating RPM. If the idle jet is restricted, the engine cannot pull enough air-fuel mixture to sustain power at lower revs, leading to stalling or severe hesitation.

You can address this by removing the carburetor and soaking the bowl in a dedicated carburetor cleaner. Do not rely on spraying cleaner while the engine runs; it rarely penetrates deep into the float bowl and often damages diaphragms in older models. A more effective approach involves disassembling the unit to clean the main jet, idle jet, and emulsion tube with a small wire or compressed air. If the carburetor is a rebuildable type, installing new gaskets and jets that match your specific model year will ensure proper flow characteristics without altering the fuel mixture beyond factory specifications.

Another common oversight involves the choke mechanism. On many 7 hp Briggs & Stratton engines, the choke lever can stick in the partially closed position due to lack of lubrication or internal corrosion. If the air intake is restricted even when you believe the mower is in "run" mode, the engine will run rich and struggle under load. Inspect the cable tension and ensure the choke plate moves freely between fully open and fully closed positions during startup.

Air filtration plays an equally significant role in maintaining peak power. A dirty air filter restricts airflow, forcing the carburetor to enrich the mixture to compensate for reduced oxygen intake. This results in a sluggish engine that bogs down immediately when the blade hits dense turf. Check the foam element; if it appears black and greasy or does not spring back after washing, replace it. Installing an aftermarket oiled cotton gauze filter can sometimes improve airflow slightly compared to standard paper filters, but only if your operating environment is low-dust. Ensure you re-oil the gauze according to manufacturer guidelines to prevent fire hazards.

Finally, consider the physical load on the deck itself. Even with a sharp blade, an unevenly balanced deck can cause vibration and drag. Use a straight edge to check the height of each corner wheel; if one side is significantly lower, the cutting cylinder will scrape against grass that should be flying off cleanly. Adjusting the deck level ensures the engine isn't fighting unnecessary friction from clippings being dragged rather than chopped.

If you have verified clean fuel lines, a functioning carburetor, and balanced geometry yet still experience power loss, the issue may lie within the ignition system or the governor linkage. A weak spark plug can fail to ignite the mixture efficiently under high load, while a disconnected governor cable might prevent the engine from reaching its full throttle setting when the throttle lever is engaged. In these cases, consulting a service manual for your specific serial number range is necessary before attempting further disassembly.
